claims.text: A thin tungsten interlayer can serve as a transition material between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep in HEA multilayers.
A tungsten interlayer alters interface coherency in HEA multilayers.
A tungsten interlayer alters lattice strain at HEA multilayer interfaces.
Equiatomic NiCrFeCoMn is an FCC HEA that can form the layers in the proposed multilayer system.
The initial HEA multilayer has coherent interfaces before introduction of tungsten.
The tungsten layer introduces localized lattice mismatch at the interfaces.
Diffusion-mediated creep dominates in the original highly coherent multilayer at lower stresses and/or temperatures.
Tungsten has strong atomic bonding.
Tungsten has a high melting point.
Inserting tungsten makes the HEA multilayer interface less coherent.
The tungsten-induced interface change suppresses atomic diffusion along the interface.
The tungsten-induced interface change facilitates dislocation nucleation at sufficiently high stress or temperature.
Suppressing interfacial diffusion and facilitating dislocation nucleation shifts creep toward dislocation-mediated behavior.
Under identical creep conditions, tungsten-containing multilayers will exhibit higher creep activation energies than multilayers without tungsten.
Under identical creep conditions, tungsten-containing multilayers will exhibit higher stress exponents than multilayers without tungsten.
Lower activation energies and stress exponents mark diffusion-mediated creep, whereas higher values mark dislocation-mediated creep in this system.
HEA multilayers without a tungsten interlayer predominantly exhibit diffusion-mediated creep under the proposed test conditions.
The proposed creep-mechanism transition occurs only near an optimal tungsten interlayer thickness.
A tungsten interlayer that is too thick or too thin may fail to induce the intended creep-mechanism shift.
The transition is limited to a temperature and stress range in which diffusion and dislocation creep can compete.
